_what: Median days between repeat purchases per RSC consumable, normalised per unit bought. The evidence base for any claim about how long a bundle lasts.
_derived: 2026-07-27, from a paginated pull of ~1,250 paid Shopify orders (all time), grouping line items by customer and product handle.
_these_are_upper_bounds: A reorder gap is consumption time PLUS however long the customer waited, lapsed, or bought elsewhere.
True duration is <= these numbers, never more. So a supply claim at or under the binding rate is defensible;
a claim ABOVE it is not defensible by this data under any reading.
The error is asymmetric in the same direction as the subscription-cadence rule: overstating supply costs the
customer and is the documented reason RSC subscribers churned. When uncertain, claim SHORT.

Where a rate carries `supersedes`, the merchant has given a direct consumption figure and it wins. A reorder gap cannot see consumption; it can only bound it. Prefer product knowledge over a weak gap every time — the deodorant's 90-day gap read as 12 months of supply for a 4-pack and was used to call a subscription plan 3x too aggressive, which was wrong.

ALL FIVE gap-derived rates in this file have now been corrected by the merchant: deodorant 90 -> 42, bar soap 47 -> 25, lotion 38 -> 30, cream 28 -> 30, toothpaste 61 -> 45. Five for five. A reorder gap measures when somebody got round to buying again, not how long the product lasted, and at this store's volume - ~16 Shopify orders/month at an ~18% repeat rate - the interval counts behind these medians were far too small to bound anything either. There is no gap-derived rate left here. If a NEW rate is ever derived that way, treat it as a hypothesis to put to the merchant, not as evidence for a claim. Note also that toothpaste carries perPerson: true - a shared product's duration depends on household size.
_how_to_use: A bundle lasts as long as the FIRST thing in it runs out — the minimum over its components of (per-unit days x quantity), not the average and not the longest. lib/supply-duration.js does this; do not re-derive it by hand.
_rederive: orders(first:250, query:"financial_status:paid") WITH pagination. lib/shopify.js getOrders() truncates at 250 silently and must not be used for this.

supersedes.why: That 38 was a median REORDER GAP over 76 intervals, not consumption. Sean, 2026-08-30: each lotion and each cream is estimated to last one month. He also named why the gap method cannot carry this claim here at all - at ~16 Shopify orders/month with an ~18% repeat rate the interval sample is far too thin to bound consumption, so a gap is not even a reliable CEILING at this store's volume, which is a stronger caveat than the one this file already carried.

That 28 was a median REORDER GAP over 24 intervals, not consumption. Sean, 2026-08-30: one month per unit. Note the direction - this rate moved UP, which a pure upper-bound reading of reorder gaps says cannot happen. That reading assumes the gap sample is meaningful; at 24 intervals on a store doing ~16 orders/month it is noise, not a bound. Third and fourth merchant corrections of gap-derived rates, after deodorant 90->42 and bar soap 47->25.

That 47 was a median REORDER GAP over 14 intervals, not consumption. Sean, 2026-08-02: 'A bar of soap is lasting between 20 and 30 days in the shower.' 25 is the midpoint; the range is kept because a bar's life genuinely varies with how many people use it.

That 61 was a median REORDER GAP over 12 intervals (confidence: weak), not consumption. Sean, 2026-08-30: 45 days per tube FOR ONE PERSON. Read that qualifier before using this rate: unlike a lotion, a tube of toothpaste is typically shared, so a two-person household consumes one in roughly half the time. A duration claim on a toothpaste bundle is therefore a claim about household size as much as about supply - state it per person, or size it for the larger household. This is the LAST gap-derived rate in this file; every one of the five has now been corrected by the merchant.

coconut-oil-toothpaste._perPersonNote: 45 days assumes a single user. Divide by the number of people brushing from the same tube before making a duration claim.

supersedes.why: That 90 was a median REORDER GAP over 8 intervals, not consumption. Sean, 2026-08-02: 'There is no way a 2oz deodorant roll on lasts 3 months, six weeks max.' A 42-day use period followed by ~7 weeks of not getting round to reordering produces a 90-day gap exactly, so the measurement and the correction do not conflict — the measurement was always an upper bound and this is the actual figure.

_no_data.coconut-oil-lip-balm: No repeat-purchase intervals. Sold as a four-pack, which further confuses per-unit rate.
